**The Weight of a Single Word**

There’s a moment, just before dawn, when the world holds its breath. The air is thick with the kind of silence that isn’t empty—it’s full, like a glass brimming with something unseen. I’ve always loved that moment. It’s the only time I feel like I can hear my own thoughts without the noise of the day drowning them out.

But thoughts are slippery things. They coil around themselves, twist into knots, and sometimes, no matter how hard you try, they refuse to be pinned down. That’s the problem with words—they’re supposed to be the net we use to catch those thoughts, but more often than not, they slip through the mesh.

I’ve been thinking about that lately. About how we use words to build bridges, only to realize too late that the other side was never there. Or how we carve them into stone, believing they’ll last forever, only to watch them erode under the weight of time. Words are powerful, but they’re also fragile. A single misplaced syllable can unravel an entire conversation. A pause too long can turn a confession into a lie.

Take the word *love*, for example. Four letters, one syllable, and yet it carries the weight of empires. We throw it around like it’s nothing—*I love this song, I love that shirt, I love the way the rain sounds on the roof*—until the moment we mean it, and suddenly, it’s too heavy to say out loud. Or worse, we say it, and the other person hears something else entirely. *Love* becomes *need*, *desire* becomes *obsession*, and before you know it, the word that was supposed to bring you closer has built a wall between you.

Then there are the words we don’t say. The ones that sit in the back of our throats, burning. *I’m sorry. I was wrong. I’m scared.* We swallow them down because saying them would mean admitting something about ourselves we’re not ready to face. Or because we’re afraid of what the other person will say in return. Silence, in those moments, feels safer. But silence has a weight of its own. It presses down on your chest until you can’t breathe, until the words you didn’t say become louder than the ones you did.

I’ve always been fascinated by the way words shape us. The stories we tell ourselves about who we are, the narratives we construct to make sense of the chaos. We’re all just collections of words, really—memories strung together like beads on a thread, each one a story we’ve chosen to keep. But what happens when the thread snaps? What happens when the words we’ve built our lives on turn out to be lies?

I remember the first time I realized that. I was twelve, sitting in a classroom, listening to my teacher explain how language evolves. She said that words change meaning over time, that the way we use them now might not be the way they were used a hundred years ago. *Awful* used to mean *full of awe*. *Nice* meant *foolish*. *Bully* was once a term of endearment. I sat there, stunned, as if someone had just told me the sky wasn’t really blue. If words could change so much, what did that mean for the stories I’d been telling myself? If the meaning of *love* could shift, what did that say about the love I thought I knew?

It’s a question I’ve been chasing ever since. Not just about love, but about all of it—*home, family, success, failure*. What do those words even mean when the definitions keep slipping through your fingers? Maybe that’s why we cling to them so tightly. Because if we let go, even for a second, we might realize that the stories we’ve been telling ourselves were never true in the first place.

But here’s the thing about words: they’re not just tools. They’re alive. They breathe, they grow, they change. And sometimes, when you least expect it, they find their way back to you. Maybe not in the way you thought they would, but in a way that makes sense. Like a song you haven’t heard in years suddenly playing on the radio, or a phrase you read in a book that lands in your chest like a stone.

I’ve been trying to write more lately. Not for anyone else, just for myself. To see if I can catch those slippery thoughts before they disappear. It’s harder than I thought it would be. Words don’t always come when you call them. Sometimes they hide, or they come out all wrong, or they arrive in a flood when you’re not ready. But I keep trying, because I think there’s something important in the act of reaching for them. Even if you never quite catch what you’re after, the reaching itself changes you.

Maybe that’s the point. Maybe words aren’t meant to be caught. Maybe they’re meant to be chased, like fireflies in the dark. You’ll never hold onto them for long, but for a moment, when they’re glowing in your palm, you remember what it feels like to believe in something.

I don’t know. Maybe I’m just tired. Maybe I’m overthinking it. But I keep coming back to that moment before dawn, when the world is quiet and anything feels possible. If I could say one true thing in that silence, what would it be?

I don’t know yet. But I think I’m getting closer.
